passage:
Sangeeta: Rhea is so upset about the trip money. Not my fault the bus tickets went up
Ayesha: You said you'd book them a week ago
Sangeeta: Not my fault the site kept crashing
Ayesha: And the missed rehearsal last month was "not my fault, the alarm didn't ring"
Sangeeta: because it wasn't??
Ayesha: Maybe partly! But the group paid extra because the tickets were booked late. Can we say that part out loud?
Sangeeta: ...I did leave it till the last night
Ayesha: Thanks for saying it. Could you tell Rhea that?
Sangeeta: ugh. fine. I feel awful
Ayesha: Awful is what owning it feels like at first. I'll wait with you 🙂

qa.q: What did Sangeeta first say about the bus tickets?
qa.a: Sangeeta said the bus tickets went up, and that it was not Sangeeta's fault.

qa.q: What is Ayesha noticing and feeling as Sangeeta keeps blaming the tickets, the site and the alarm?
qa.a: Ayesha is patient but a little frustrated, having heard the same reply about the tickets, the site and the alarm, and hopes Sangeeta will own part of it.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that moved Sangeeta from an excuse toward owning the harm?
qa.a: Ayesha named the part that was Sangeeta's, the late booking, and asked to say it out loud, without accusing. Sangeeta then admitted it.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta be feeling on writing that it feels awful?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels guilty now that the late booking has been admitted, and is probably uncomfortable about telling Rhea. The excuses had kept that feeling away.

grounding: A friend hears someone say it was not my fault every time; forgiveness needs owning the harm first, and excuses skip that step.

passage:
At the tea stall in Shivpur, Vijay had noticed that whatever went wrong, Salma's answer was the same. She borrowed Bashir's bicycle and bent the wheel: "The road is bad, not my fault." Last week she left the hen-coop open and two of Kamla's hens were lost: "The latch is loose, not my fault." Each time she gave a small shrug and changed the subject.
Today Vijay asked her, gently, "Was any of it yours?"
Salma didn't answer at first. Then, "I was racing the rain on Bashir's cycle. And I didn't check the latch."
"That sounds true," Vijay said.
Her shoulders dropped. The next morning she took the wheel to the repairer with her own coins and told Bashir herself. Her face still looked tight, but she looked at him.

qa.q: Whose bicycle did Salma bend the wheel of?
qa.a: Salma bent the wheel of Bashir's bicycle.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling as Salma gave the same reply after each mishap?
qa.a: Vijay was concerned and a little puzzled, seeing the same reply every time, that it was not her fault, followed by a shrug and a new subject.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that made room for Salma to own her part?
qa.a: Vijay asked gently whether any of it was hers and, when Salma named her part, said it sounded true instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when her shoulders dropped after admitting her part?
qa.a: Salma probably felt exposed but also relieved, since the admission let her drop the shrug and act. Her tight face shows the guilt had not gone yet.

grounding: A person hears a friend say it was not my fault every time; self-forgiveness needs owning the harm, and excuses leave guilt unresolved.

passage: Felix had shared a flat in Leipzig with Clara for a year, and he'd started counting. The broken kettle: "Not my fault, it was old." The rent paid late: "Not my fault, the bank was slow." Last night she'd forgotten to lock the front door and his bike was stolen. "It's not my fault, the lock is stiff." Felix believed some of these. But he noticed that Clara never seemed lighter after saying it. She'd been snappy all morning and kept checking the empty spot where the bike had been. At lunch he said, carefully, "I'm not trying to blame you. It's just a bike." Clara put her fork down. After a long pause she said, "I forgot the door. I'm really sorry." Her voice cracked. She looked, for the first time in weeks, relieved.

qa.q: What was stolen after Clara forgot to lock the door?
qa.a: Felix's bike.

qa.q: How did Felix feel, noticing that Clara never seemed lighter after her excuses?
qa.a: Felix felt puzzled and a little concerned, sensing that the excuses were not easing her guilt.

qa.q: What did Felix say that made it easier for Clara to own the mistake?
qa.a: He said calmly that he wasn't trying to blame her and it was just a bike, which lowered the stakes enough for her to admit it.

qa.q: What was it like for Clara to finally say 'I forgot the door'?
qa.a: It was hard, since her voice cracked, but she looked relieved for the first time in weeks.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing that someone's repeated 'not my fault' leaves guilt unresolved, and that owning the harm brings relief.

passage: At the biotech lab on the third floor, Avni watched Amandeep open the freezer and go pale. The samples for their project, six weeks of work, had thawed. Amandeep had left the door ajar the night before. "It's not my fault," Amandeep said immediately. "This freezer is ancient. Someone should have fixed the seal." Avni nodded, but she'd seen the door open at seven. For the next two days Amandeep snapped at everyone, skipped the team lunch, and kept muttering about the seal. Avni wasn't sure what to say. On Thursday, while they were restarting the cultures, Amandeep stopped pipetting. "I left it open. I checked my phone and walked off." Avni just said, "Okay. Thanks for saying it." Amandeep let out a long breath. The rest of the afternoon, the snapping stopped.

qa.q: How many weeks of work had thawed in the freezer?
qa.a: Six weeks of work.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when Amandeep blamed the freezer?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy and unsure what to say, since she had seen the door open at seven.

qa.q: Why did Avni's simple reply help?
qa.a: She didn't scold or lecture; she thanked Amandeep for owning it, which let the guilt finally ease.

qa.q: How was Amandeep affected by admitting the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep let out a long breath and stopped snapping, which suggests the unresolved guilt had been weighing heavily.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that repeated excuses leave someone's guilt unresolved, and that owning the harm lets them move on.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,

I've wanted to write this for a while, and it's easier on paper.

When you missed my birthday dinner, you said the auto driver got lost. When you forgot to return my exam notes before the test, you said your mother had moved them. When you told Sneha what I'd shared in confidence, you said, "It's not my fault, she asked me directly."

Maybe some of those are true. But I've noticed you look more stressed every time you say it, not less. It's like the excuse stops the conversation before anything can be put right.

I'm not angry anymore. I just miss how we used to be. If you ever want to say "I messed up," I'll be here to hear it, and I'll forgive you faster than you think.

Mehak

qa.q: What did Minakshi say about telling Sneha what Mehak shared?
qa.a: Minakshi said, 'It's not my fault, she asked me directly.'

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about the excuses?
qa.a: Mehak seems sad and missing the old friendship, no longer angry but worried that the excuses keep Minakshi stressed.

qa.q: What small step does Mehak invite Minakshi to take?
qa.a: To simply say 'I messed up', which would let them repair things and let Minakshi forgive herself.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Minakshi might feel exposed and defensive at first, but perhaps relieved that Mehak is ready to forgive.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone's repeated excuses skip owning the harm and leave the guilt unresolved.

passage: You want to know why I stopped arguing with Pema? I'm Nazia, his lab partner since first year, so I've heard it all. When he borrowed Tenzin's scooter and scraped it, it was the gravel's fault. When our group missed the project deadline because his part never came, it was the Wi-Fi. When he forgot Dechen's birthday, it was "you didn't remind me". Every time: "Not my fault." The funny thing is, he keeps bringing these things up. Late at night he'll say, "Tenzin's still weird with me, no?" So it clearly sits on him. Last week I just asked, "What was your part in it?" He was quiet so long I thought he'd hung up. Then he said, "I rode too fast." First time I've ever heard him say that. I think it was a relief for him.

qa.q: What did Pema blame for the scraped scooter?
qa.a: Pema said it was the gravel's fault.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Pema kept bringing up Tenzin?
qa.a: Nazia felt puzzled and a little frustrated, noticing that the guilt clearly still weighed on him despite all the excuses.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's question work better than arguing?
qa.a: Asking about his part invited Pema to own the harm himself, the step his excuses had always skipped.

qa.q: How might Pema feel after saying "I rode too fast"?
qa.a: He might feel exposed but lighter, since owning the harm finally gives the guilt somewhere to go.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone's constant excuses leave his guilt unresolved until he finally owns his part.
